title: 2026 - Challenge or Pass A Dynamic Policy for MLB's Automated Ball-Strike System - Pipping-Gam n et al
file_name: 2026 - Challenge or Pass A Dynamic Policy for MLB's Automated Ball-Strike System - Pipping-Gam n et al.pdf
universal_lens: A dynamic policy framework for MLB's ABS challenge system integrates run expectancy, Bayesian belief updates, and stochastic optimization to maximize strategic value. Bayesian hierarchical modeling of pitch margin distributions with shrinkage priors and sensory likelihoods for dynamic challenge policy optimization.
gsi_mapping: Bayesian inference models player perception uncertainty; conformal prediction calibrates overturn probability estimates from historical challenge data. GSI employs conformal predictive inference to compute posterior challenge probabilities using role-specific shrinkage priors and Gaussian sensory error models.
gse_mapping: Situational reasoning encodes state transitions via run expectancy changes; state-space includes count, outs, runners, and remaining challenges. GSE utilizes Markov decision processes with state-value iteration to optimize challenge decisions based on expected run gains and future challenge costs.

primitives.name: Bayesian Overturn Probability Model
primitives.verbatim_quote: A Bayesian model represents players' imperfect impressions of pitch location and uses them to estimate overturn probabilities, with uncertainty calibrated from historical challenge decisions.
primitives.latex: P(\text{overturn} \mid \theta, D) = \int P(\text{overturn} \mid \theta) P(\theta \mid D) d\theta

primitives.assumptions: Players' perceptions follow normal distribution around true pitch location; historical data provides sufficient calibration.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When pitch location is ambiguous or near boundary of strike zone.

primitives.name: Dynamic Programming Challenge Policy
primitives.verbatim_quote: Dynamic programming compares the expected gain with the future cost of losing a challenge, accounting for the stage of the game, the number of challenges remaining, and opportunities on both offense and defense.

reasoning_traces.think: This chapter introduces a formalized dynamic policy for MLB’s Automated Ball-Strike (ABS) challenge system, grounded in game-theoretic principles and empirical data. The core innovation lies in integrating run expectancy models with Bayesian inference to assess the value of overturning calls. Players face a trade-off: challenging a call risks losing a limited resource (challenges), yet failing to challenge may miss valuable corrections. The authors employ dynamic programming to optimize this trade-off across game states defined by count, outs, runners, and remaining challenges. Their Bayesian model captures the discrepancy between perceived and actual pitch locations, enabling accurate overturn probability estimation. The policy is trained on pre-2026 data and validated post-break, showing measurable gains in run correction efficiency. The framework demonstrates that strategic challenge usage improves over passive behavior, even if overturn rates decrease. This suggests that traditional metrics like overturn rate are insufficient for evaluating challenge efficacy. Instead, the value of a challenge should be assessed through its impact on expected runs, which the policy quantifies. The paper also highlights the importance of reconstructing challenge opportunities from incomplete data, including those not challenged. This reconstruction enables backtesting and validation of the proposed policy. The integration of pitch tracking, game records, and statistical modeling creates a robust foundation for real-time decision support systems in professional baseball. It bridges theoretical game theory with practical implementation, offering insights applicable to other domains requiring sequential decision-making under uncertainty.
